intro: Finding a mole check near you is a practical step when a mole has caught your attention, whether it has changed or you simply want reassurance. You want a local professional who can examine your skin properly and explain what they see. We introduce you to a suitable private consultant who can assess your moles and quote you directly.
need_heading: What people searching for a mole check usually need
need_lead: Most people looking for a mole check near them have a specific concern about a mole or their skin, and want a prompt, local appointment with someone qualified to assess it.
needs: You have noticed a mole that has changed in shape, colour or size and want it looked at without delay.
You have several moles and would like them checked as a baseline, especially if you have a family history of skin cancer or have spent time in the sun.
You are worried about a new or unusual spot on your skin and want a professional opinion close to home.
You have been advised by a GP or another clinician to have a mole checked and prefer to see a private consultant quickly.
You want the option of mole mapping to track changes over time, and need to find a local service that offers it.
context_heading: What to understand about mole checks
context: A mole check is a clinical examination, usually with a dermatoscope, to assess moles for signs of skin cancer. The consultant will look at any mole that concerns you and may recommend removal or monitoring. Suspicious moles need urgent attention, so it is important to act on any changes you have noticed.

Private consultants who carry out mole checks should appear on the GMC's specialist register for their field, which you can check online. Private clinics providing regulated healthcare in England must register with the Care Quality Commission (CQC), which inspects and publishes ratings; in Wales the regulator is Healthcare Inspectorate Wales, in Scotland Healthcare Improvement Scotland, and in Northern Ireland the RQIA. Many private specialists also work in the NHS.
tell_heading: What to tell iComply when enquiring
tell: Describe the mole or moles that concern you, including any changes in shape, colour or size you have noticed.
Mention how long you have had the mole and whether it is new or has been there for some time.
Say whether you have a family history of skin cancer or have had significant sun exposure.
Confirm your location and how far you are willing to travel for an appointment.
Note whether you have private medical insurance and if a GP referral is required by your insurer.
Mention any preference for a particular type of consultant or clinic, such as one that offers mole mapping.
questions: What does the mole check involve and will you use dermoscopy?
How will you decide whether a mole needs removal or monitoring?
What are the signs that a mole should be seen urgently?
Do you offer mole mapping to track changes over time?
Are you on the GMC's specialist register for dermatology?
Is the clinic registered with the relevant regulator, such as the CQC?

faqs.q: What happens during a mole check?
faqs.a: The consultant will examine your skin, often using a dermatoscope to look closely at moles. They will assess any mole that concerns you and may recommend removal or monitoring. Suspicious moles need urgent attention.

faqs.q: Should I see a GP first?
faqs.a: You can see a private consultant directly, but if you have private medical insurance, your insurer may require a GP referral and may limit you to certain consultants or hospitals. Check with your insurer before you book.

faqs.q: How do I check if a consultant is qualified?
faqs.a: Hospital consultants should appear on the GMC's specialist register for their field, which you can check online. You can also check whether the clinic is registered with the relevant regulator, such as the CQC in England.

faqs.q: What changes in a mole should prompt a check?
faqs.a: Look for changes in shape, colour or size. A mole that is new, itching, bleeding or not healing should be seen urgently. If you are unsure, it is safer to have it checked.
